transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman, stocks open lower as new applications
for unemployment benefits have fallen.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell about 360 points in
early trading.
Fewer people applied for unemployment benefits last week than did the week before.
Companies have been hovering at a low level, suggesting few people are being laid off in
the current economy.
That's helping to keep the unemployment rate low, even as hiring is also soft.
We'll get a more complete update on the job market tomorrow.
The stable labor markets allow the Federal Reserve to focus on fighting inflation for
now.
Investors expect the Fed to raise interest rates next month.
The Bank of England took that step today.
Wendy's reported better-than-expected profits for the most recent quarter.
And even though sales at existing restaurants were down, the burger chain rejected a $1.4
billion takeover bid from an activist investor.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
Two Senate races are still undecided from this week's midterms.
One is in Mississippi.
Democratic challenger Scott Colombe barely leads Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The other undecided Senate race is in Alaska.
Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is slightly ahead of Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
Alaska public media's Liz Ruskin has more.
Alaska, it turns out, was not key to control of the Senate.
That was called for Democrats while Alaskans were still voting.
The state counts ballots until November 18.
If no candidate wins a majority, the state will tabulate ranked choices akin to an instant
runoff.
One issue dominated the last days of the race, allegations that Peltola's team helped recruit
a second candidate named Dan Sullivan.
Peltola says she was unaware.
Meanwhile, the Justice Department is appealing the dismissal of a lawsuit to withhold the
election certification if Senator Sullivan narrowly loses.
For NPR News, I'm Liz Ruskin in Anchorage.
President Trump weighed in online this morning.
He says votes for the "fake" Dan Sullivan should be given to GOP incumbent Senator Dan
Sullivan.
Trump claims that's how the incumbent Republican senator would win.
Meanwhile, Democrats continue to celebrate their major congressional wins.
NPR's Barbara Sprunt reports the election is seen as a referendum of Trump's policies.
President Trump endorsed some candidates this cycle that raised eyebrows among Republicans.
In Texas, where he insisted on embattled Attorney General Ken Paxton over the incumbent Senator
John Cornyn, Trump asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot this cycle in order to
boost turnout.
But with sagging approval ratings and policies that voters linked to their cost of living
concerns like tariffs in the Iran war, the president may have hurt Republican candidates
more than he helped.
Barbara Sprunt and PR News, Washington.
Stock prices continue to plunge.
The Nasdaq is down more than 3 percent.
It's NPR.
The White House says First Lady Melania Trump will host representatives from Russia and
Ukraine today.
They're supposed to talk about a recent ceasefire she helped broker in a Ukrainian town near
the front lines.
Hundreds of civilians were able to leave for other parts of Ukraine or for Russia.
Mrs. Trump's effort comes ahead of U.S.-led peace talks next week.
A new report finds a record share of first-time homebuyers are paying with all cash.
And bears Jennifer Ludden explains that a key to that is getting an inheritance.
One in 10 first-time homebuyers pay all cash, according to the National Association of Realtors,
and more than a quarter of them use inherited money.
And they are deputy chief economist Jessica Lautz, as they're also significantly older
than traditional first-time buyers with a median age of 54.
They waited a significant period of time for that generational transfer of wealth to come
through.
Real estate agents say intense competition and sky-high interest rates are driving all
cash offers.
And, of course, some families don't wait until death to pass on money.
The report notes it's all widening the divide between homebuyers and those priced out.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News, Washington.
The Vatican says that Pope Leo will leave tomorrow for a long-planned trip to South America.
He is still being cared for by doctors after his lung cancer surgery last month.
Doctors removed part of the pontiff's right lung.
But they say he is recovering well.
They say no further surgical treatment is needed.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Stocks open lower as jobless claims fall and Dow drops about 360 points
Bank of England raises interest rates; Fed expected to raise rates next month
Wendy's beats profit expectations but rejects $1.4 billion takeover bid from activist investor
Mississippi Senate race undecided as Democrat Scott Colombe narrowly leads Cindy Hyde-Smith
Alaska Senate race undecided; Mary Peltola slightly ahead of Dan Sullivan, count continues to November 18
Trump claims votes for 'fake' Dan Sullivan should go to incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan
Democrats celebrate midterm wins seen as referendum on Trump policies and cost of living
Melania Trump to host Russian and Ukrainian representatives after civilian evacuation ceasefire in Ukraine
Record share of first-time homebuyers paying all cash, many using inherited money
Pope Leo to leave for South America trip despite recovering from lung cancer surgery
